catalog_quote: Stress refers to the emphasis given to a particular syllable. The loudness of a syllable characterizes it. The symbol [‘] is used in this study as a symbol for stress. This symbol is placed before the stressed syllable. As shown in the examples below, word or lexical stress in Higaonon is phonemic. When the placement of the stress changes, the meaning of the word also changes. [‘sa.la] ‘punishment’ / [sa.’la] ‘sin’ / [‘su.ləd] ‘sibling’ / [su.’ləd] ‘inside’. Meanwhile, stress is placed on the ultimate or penultimate syllable of Higaonon words. Stress on the ultimate syllable: [tun.’lo] ‘finger’, [tə.’ŋəl] ‘nape’, [pi.’lək] ‘eyelash’, [ku.’diŋ] ‘cat’. Stress on the penultimate syllable: [‘ba.he] ‘woman’, [‘ka.ʔən] ‘eat’, [‘kag.pa] ‘chest’, [‘su.lo] ‘fingernail’. ... [Conclusion, p. 64] Word stress in this language is phonemic.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is contrastive (phonemic): it falls on either the final or the penultimate syllable of the word and its position is not predictable from the segmental shape, as shown by minimal pairs distinguished by stress alone (sala 'punishment' vs sala 'sin'; suled 'sibling' vs suled 'inside'). The source gives no default position, no weight or morphological conditioning, and no statement about which position is more common; the window is the last two syllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned anywhere in the article.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the description is example-based (four ultimate, four penultimate, two minimal pairs) and states only that stress is placed on the ultimate or penultimate syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: the section is titled 'Word Stress', speaks of 'word or lexical stress' and 'Higaonon words', and the data are elicited citation-form words and sentences collected from tribal leaders of the Opol (Misamis Oriental) variety; nothing on phrase-level or affixed-form stress.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement describes the Higaonon variety of Opol, Misamis Oriental (data from Opol tribal leaders), explicitly labelled Higaonon [ISO 639-3 mba] = Glottolog higa1237. Abingosa et al. note (citing KWF 2023) that vowel phonemes differ between Bukidnon/Claveria varieties and other Higaonon communities, so the ult/penult contrast is attested for Opol only. Closely related Binukid (Talaandig-Binukid, binu1244, 77-81% intelligibility) is already in the catalog from Post & Gardner 1992 with the same phonemic-stress pattern (sala/sala minimal pair, usually penult); Glottolog keeps the two as separate languoids under 'Bukidnon'.

new_statements.relation_note: Weak, independent corroboration only: the 1973 Minalwang (Gingoog) wordlist's pre-syllable stress strokes fall on both penultimate and final syllables, consistent with the catalog record (Abingosa et al. 2026, Opol variety: 'word or lexical stress in Higaonon is phonemic.. placed on the ultimate or penultimate syllable'). It adds no rule, no minimal pair and no statement; the documents that would state the system (Munger 1985 Phonemic statement, SIL 43457; Munger 1986 Morphophonemic changes, 43458; Grammar Essentials 68866) remain unread and are browser-hand-download only (no archived copy at the Internet Archive exists). The 2017 spelling guides are silent on stress (agreeing with the 2026…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No document in the held SIL set STATES a stress rule. The 1973 re-typed 1966-schedule wordlist (SIL 79461) marks a subset of items (c. 35 of 372) with a raised stroke placed BEFORE a syllable; because it stands word-initially before consonants ('balay, 'kilat, 'babuy, 'wahig) it cannot be a glottal-stop sign (final glottal stop is written with a grave: batà-type sudà, punù), and by the usual IPA/SIL survey convention it marks the stressed syllable. Read that way, stress falls on the penult in 'babuy, 'bayad, 'wahig, 'takaw, 'pitu, ka'wanan, u'lunà, a'yamà, ma'nipis and on the final syllable in u'taw, u'dan, a'sin, la'lang, tu'bu, ba'bà, pi'sà, nga'dug, i.e. on either of the last two syllables of segmentally parallel shapes (u'dan vs 'wahig, a'sin vs 'atup), which is what the catalog's source (Abingosa et al. 2026) states in prose: phonemic stress on the ultimate or penultimate syllable. This is an inference from unmarked-convention transcription, hence confidence low. The two 2017 DepEd/SIL spelling guides (Higaunon 74554, Banwaon 74596) give only orthographic rules (syllable template, glottal stop written with grave accent or hyphen) and say nothing about stress; the Banwaon handwritten list (80080) has no stress prose.
new_statements.secondary_stress: nothing (no secondary marks in the wordlist; no prose anywhere in the held set)
new_statements.exceptions: none stated; three items carry a non-final grave (nàmatay 68, màdalom 71, ùsa 72) of undetermined meaning (typist's rendering of a stress mark or of the handwritten original's accent); items 141 mapasu' and 198 huda' carry a trailing apostrophe (probably final glottal stop, cf. 202 hudà)
new_statements.identity_note: The held wordlist SIL 79461 is Higaonon of Minalwang (Minalowang), Gingoog, Misamis Oriental (collector/informant Vicente Mansancagan, 1966 schedule, re-typed 1973); the catalog source describes Higaonon of Opol, Misamis Oriental; Munger's unread manuscripts describe Higaonon of Bandahan, Misamis Oriental. SIL files Banwaon (Agusan del Sur; guides 74596, lists 79692/80080) under the same ISO code [mba]; the Banwaon items were checked but say nothing on stress.
